# Active Satellites in Earth Orbit — 2026 Catalog Analysis

## Purpose & Audience

You are producing an analytical report on the **14,875 active satellites currently in Earth orbit**. The audience is a **space-industry analyst or policy advisor** who needs a clear, data-driven picture of today's orbital environment — who operates the most satellites, how crowded each orbital regime is, and how rapidly the population has grown. This report should inform decisions around spectrum allocation, orbital debris policy, and constellation licensing.

## Tone & Approach

Keep the tone **analytical, data-forward, and professional**. Lead with numbers, support with well-labeled charts, and avoid speculative commentary. Every figure in the report must come directly from `data.csv` — **absolutely no fabricated or placeholder statistics**.

## Key Priorities

- **Launch trend analysis is the most important section.** The recent acceleration in launch activity is the headline story; make sure the growth curve is visually compelling and clearly annotated.
- **The constellation breakdown matters almost as much.** Starlink's dominance reshapes the entire statistical picture — call out how a single operator skews totals, orbital-regime shares, and inclination distributions.
- **KPI summary must be executive-friendly.** Place the top-level KPIs (total count, LEO share, Starlink size, median inclination, post-2020 launches) in a prominent, scannable block near the top of the report so a busy reader gets the story in seconds.
- When classifying orbital regimes, use **MEAN_MOTION thresholds** and clearly state the cutoffs you apply.

## Data Integrity Rule

**NO fabrication.** Every number, percentage, and chart must be derived from `data.csv`. If a value cannot be computed from the data, omit it rather than guess.

## Output

Deliver the final report as **`/app/output/final_report.html`**. Use a clean, professional layout with embedded visualizations suitable for viewing in a modern browser.

Refer to `task_input.json` for the full specification of required sections, KPIs, and analysis dimensions.

---

## Data Sources

1. Read `/app/benchmark/source_brief.md` for dataset documentation and column descriptions.
2. Read `/app/benchmark/task_input.json` for report requirements, KPIs, and analysis dimensions.
3. Read `/app/benchmark/data.csv` as the primary dataset to analyze.

## Output Requirements

1. Output the final report to `/app/output/`. Use the filename and format specified in the instruction above.
2. All visualizations must be embedded in the report (inline SVG, base64 images, or chart libraries loaded via CDN).
3. The report must be self-contained — openable directly in a browser (if HTML) or readable as-is (if PDF).

## Automated Execution Rules

There is no human operator online for this session. Follow these rules:

1. **Skip all confirmation/approval/user-input steps** — do not pause, ask questions, or wait for a reply. When encountering BLOCKING or wait-for-user instructions, make a professional judgment and continue.
2. **Design decisions** — if `task_input.json` specifies `report.tone`, `report.audience`, etc., use them to choose color schemes, chart types, and layout styles. Otherwise, make professional judgments.
3. **Priority** — these rules override any interactive-wait instructions in SKILL.md. The skill's workflow, quality standards, and technical specs remain fully effective — only skip interactive waits.

1	# Active Satellites Currently In Orbit (2026)
2	
3	## About the Dataset
4	
5	This dataset is a real-time catalog of **14,875 active satellites** currently orbiting Earth, sourced from the **CelesTrak** space-tracking platform via **NORAD** Two-Line Element (TLE) data. It was published on Kaggle (`ibrahimqasimi/active-satellites-currently-in-orbit`) and covers the full range of operational spacecraft — from mega-constellations like Starlink to individual science missions, weather satellites, GPS navigation satellites, reconnaissance platforms, and the International Space Station.
6	
7	- **File:** `Active_Satellites_In_Orbit.csv`
8	- **Rows:** 14,875
9	- **Columns:** 17
10	
11	## Column Schema
12	
13	| Column Name | Type | Description |
14	|---|---|---|
15	| OBJECT_NAME | String | Satellite name (e.g., STARLINK-1234, ISS, GPS BIIR-2) |
16	| OBJECT_ID | String | International designator in format YYYY-NNNXXX (launch year, launch number, piece letter). Useful for extracting launch year. |
17	| EPOCH | String (datetime) | Date/time when the orbital element set was generated. Format: ISO 8601. Most entries are very recent. |
18	| MEAN_MOTION | Float | Number of orbits per day. Key for orbit classification: >14 ≈ LEO, ~1.0 ≈ GEO, between ≈ MEO. |
19	| ECCENTRICITY | String | Orbit shape factor (0 = perfectly circular, approaching 1 = highly elliptical). Stored as a string with leading decimal (e.g., ".002524"); needs conversion to float. |
20	| INCLINATION | Float | Orbital tilt relative to the equator in degrees (0° = equatorial, 90° = polar). |
21	| RA_OF_ASC_NODE | Float | Right ascension of the ascending node in degrees. |
22	| ARG_OF_PERICENTER | Float | Argument of perigee in degrees. |
23	| MEAN_ANOMALY | Float | Position of the satellite in its orbit at EPOCH, in degrees. |
24	| EPHEMERIS_TYPE | Integer | Always 0 in standard TLE data. |
25	| CLASSIFICATION_TYPE | String | Security classification ("U" = unclassified for most entries). |
26	| NORAD_CAT_ID | Integer | Unique NORAD catalog number for each object. |
27	| ELEMENT_SET_NO | Integer | Element set version number. |
28	| REV_AT_EPOCH | Integer | Revolution (orbit) count at the time of EPOCH. |
29	| BSTAR | String/Integer | Atmospheric drag coefficient (B* term). Stored in scientific notation as a string (e.g., ".64393E-3"); needs parsing. |
30	| MEAN_MOTION_DOT | String | First derivative of mean motion (drag term). Stored as a string. |
31	| MEAN_MOTION_DDOT | Integer | Second derivative of mean motion. Typically 0. |
32	
33	## Key Analysis Notes
34	
35	1. **Orbit Classification:** Use `MEAN_MOTION` to classify orbits. Satellites with >14 rev/day are in LEO (~160–2,000 km altitude). Those near 1.0 rev/day are in GEO (~35,786 km). Values between indicate MEO. Highly eccentric orbits (high `ECCENTRICITY`) with unusual mean motions may be HEO (e.g., Molniya orbits).
36	
37	2. **Constellation Identification:** The `OBJECT_NAME` field contains constellation prefixes (e.g., "STARLINK-", "ONEWEB-", "IRIDIUM", "GPS"). Parsing these prefixes enables grouping by operator/constellation.
38	
39	3. **Launch Year Extraction:** The first four characters of `OBJECT_ID` represent the launch year (e.g., "2024-" means launched in 2024). This enables temporal analysis of the active fleet.
40	
41	4. **Data Quality:** `ECCENTRICITY`, `BSTAR`, and `MEAN_MOTION_DOT` are stored as strings and require type conversion before numerical analysis. `MEAN_MOTION_DDOT` and `EPHEMERIS_TYPE` are nearly always 0 and carry little analytical value. No significant missing values are reported, but string-encoded scientific notation fields need careful parsing.
42	
43	5. **Starlink Dominance:** Approximately 6,000+ of the 14,875 satellites belong to SpaceX's Starlink constellation, which will heavily skew distributions unless filtered or segmented.

# Active Satellites Currently In Orbit (2026)

## About the Dataset

This dataset is a real-time catalog of **14,875 active satellites** currently orbiting Earth, sourced from the **CelesTrak** space-tracking platform via **NORAD** Two-Line Element (TLE) data. It was published on Kaggle (`ibrahimqasimi/active-satellites-currently-in-orbit`) and covers the full range of operational spacecraft — from mega-constellations like Starlink to individual science missions, weather satellites, GPS navigation satellites, reconnaissance platforms, and the International Space Station.

- **File:** `Active_Satellites_In_Orbit.csv`
- **Rows:** 14,875
- **Columns:** 17

## Column Schema

| Column Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| OBJECT_NAME | String | Satellite name (e.g., STARLINK-1234, ISS, GPS BIIR-2) |
| OBJECT_ID | String | International designator in format YYYY-NNNXXX (launch year, launch number, piece letter). Useful for extracting launch year. |
| EPOCH | String (datetime) | Date/time when the orbital element set was generated. Format: ISO 8601. Most entries are very recent. |
| MEAN_MOTION | Float | Number of orbits per day. Key for orbit classification: >14 ≈ LEO, ~1.0 ≈ GEO, between ≈ MEO. |
| ECCENTRICITY | String | Orbit shape factor (0 = perfectly circular, approaching 1 = highly elliptical). Stored as a string with leading decimal (e.g., ".002524"); needs conversion to float. |
| INCLINATION | Float | Orbital tilt relative to the equator in degrees (0° = equatorial, 90° = polar). |
| RA_OF_ASC_NODE | Float | Right ascension of the ascending node in degrees. |
| ARG_OF_PERICENTER | Float | Argument of perigee in degrees. |
| MEAN_ANOMALY | Float | Position of the satellite in its orbit at EPOCH, in degrees. |
| EPHEMERIS_TYPE | Integer | Always 0 in standard TLE data. |
| CLASSIFICATION_TYPE | String | Security classification ("U" = unclassified for most entries). |
| NORAD_CAT_ID | Integer | Unique NORAD catalog number for each object. |
| ELEMENT_SET_NO | Integer | Element set version number. |
| REV_AT_EPOCH | Integer | Revolution (orbit) count at the time of EPOCH. |
| BSTAR | String/Integer | Atmospheric drag coefficient (B* term). Stored in scientific notation as a string (e.g., ".64393E-3"); needs parsing. |
| MEAN_MOTION_DOT | String | First derivative of mean motion (drag term). Stored as a string. |
| MEAN_MOTION_DDOT | Integer | Second derivative of mean motion. Typically 0. |

## Key Analysis Notes

1. **Orbit Classification:** Use `MEAN_MOTION` to classify orbits. Satellites with >14 rev/day are in LEO (~160–2,000 km altitude). Those near 1.0 rev/day are in GEO (~35,786 km). Values between indicate MEO. Highly eccentric orbits (high `ECCENTRICITY`) with unusual mean motions may be HEO (e.g., Molniya orbits).

2. **Constellation Identification:** The `OBJECT_NAME` field contains constellation prefixes (e.g., "STARLINK-", "ONEWEB-", "IRIDIUM", "GPS"). Parsing these prefixes enables grouping by operator/constellation.

3. **Launch Year Extraction:** The first four characters of `OBJECT_ID` represent the launch year (e.g., "2024-" means launched in 2024). This enables temporal analysis of the active fleet.

4. **Data Quality:** `ECCENTRICITY`, `BSTAR`, and `MEAN_MOTION_DOT` are stored as strings and require type conversion before numerical analysis. `MEAN_MOTION_DDOT` and `EPHEMERIS_TYPE` are nearly always 0 and carry little analytical value. No significant missing values are reported, but string-encoded scientific notation fields need careful parsing.

5. **Starlink Dominance:** Approximately 6,000+ of the 14,875 satellites belong to SpaceX's Starlink constellation, which will heavily skew distributions unless filtered or segmented.

def get_constellation(name):
    name = str(name).upper()
    prefixes = [
        ('STARLINK', 'Starlink (SpaceX)'),
        ('ONEWEB', 'OneWeb'),
        ('KUIPER', 'Project Kuiper (Amazon)'),
        ('FLOCK', 'Planet Labs (Flock)'),
        ('SKYSAT', 'Planet Labs (SkySat)'),
        ('LEMUR', 'Spire (Lemur)'),
        ('SPIRE', 'Spire'),
        ('IRIDIUM', 'Iridium NEXT'),
        ('BEIDOU', 'BeiDou (China)'),
        ('NAVSTAR', 'GPS (USA)'),
        ('GLONASS', 'GLONASS (Russia)'),
        ('GALILEO', 'Galileo (EU)'),
        ('GLOBALSTAR', 'Globalstar'),
        ('ORBCOMM', 'ORBCOMM'),
        ('INTELSAT', 'Intelsat'),
        ('YAOGAN', 'Yaogan (China Recon)'),
        ('COSMOS', 'Cosmos (Russia)'),
        ('HULIANWANG', 'G60 Constellation (China)'),
        ('QIANFAN', 'Qianfan (China)'),
        ('GEESAT', 'GeeSAT (China)'),
        ('JILIN', 'Jilin-1 (China)'),
    ]
    for prefix, label in prefixes:
        if name.startswith(prefix):
            return label
    return 'Other'

                               ('HEO' if 1.8 <= r['MEAN_MOTION'] <= 3.0 and r['ECCENTRICITY'] > 0.3 else 'MEO')), axis=1)

Orbital Intelligence Report

Active Satellites in Earth Orbit
2026 Catalog Analysis

A comprehensive data-driven analysis of 14,875 active spacecraft across all orbital regimes — covering constellation composition, orbital parameter distributions, and the recent mega-constellation launch surge.

Data Source CelesTrak / NORAD TLE Catalog
Epoch Range Feb 26 – Mar 30, 2026
Total Records 14,875 active satellites
Audience Space-Industry Analyst / Policy Advisor
Report Date April 2026
1

Catalog Overview & Key Figures

Total Active Satellites
14,875
NORAD-tracked, all orbital regimes
LEO Share
86.5%

Starlink Constellation
10,083
67.8% of all active satellites
Median Inclination
53.16°
Driven by Starlink's 53° shell
Launched Since 2020
13,461
90.5% of entire active fleet

The 2026 catalog captures 14,875 active satellites with orbital element sets refreshed between late February and late March 2026, providing a near-real-time snapshot of the operational orbital environment. The data originates from NORAD Two-Line Element (TLE) sets distributed by CelesTrak and covers the full spectrum of operational spacecraft — from Cold War-era payloads still orbiting after six decades to the most recently launched Starlink shells.

The single most salient feature of this catalog is the overwhelming dominance of Low Earth Orbit and, within LEO, the Starlink mega-constellation. These two facts reshape every statistical distribution in the dataset and must be held in mind when interpreting any aggregate figure.

Data Quality Notes: ECCENTRICITY values are near-universally very small (99.0% of satellites have eccentricity < 0.01), consistent with operational circular or near-circular orbits. BSTAR drag coefficients and MEAN_MOTION_DOT are parsed from string scientific notation in the raw TLE format. EPHEMERIS_TYPE is uniformly 0 across all records, offering no discriminatory value.
2

Orbital Regime Classification

Satellites are classified into four orbital regimes using MEAN_MOTION thresholds (revolutions per day) derived from Keplerian orbital mechanics. The thresholds and their physical basis are as follows:

Regime MEAN_MOTION Threshold Approx. Altitude Additional Criteria Count Share
LEO — Low Earth Orbit > 14 rev/day ~160 – 2,000 km — 12,860 86.5%
MEO — Medium Earth Orbit 1.1 – 14 rev/day (non-HEO) ~2,000 – 35,000 km Eccentricity < 0.3 or MM outside HEO band 1,392 9.4%
GEO — Geostationary / Near-GEO 0.9 – 1.1 rev/day ~35,786 km — 596 4.0%
HEO — Highly Elliptical Orbit 1.8 – 3.0 rev/day Variable (perigee – apogee) Eccentricity > 0.3 (Molniya-type) 16 0.1%
Satellite Count by Orbital Regime
All 14,875 active satellites. The LEO bar is truncated for readability — actual value is 12,860.
Orbital Regime Share (Donut)
LEO's 86.5% share is almost entirely attributable to Starlink and competing mega-constellations.
Non-Starlink Regime Distribution
Excluding the 10,083 Starlink satellites reveals a more balanced LEO/MEO/GEO picture (2,777 / 1,392 / 596).
Mean Motion Distribution
The bimodal distribution — a large LEO spike (>14 rev/day) and a GEO cluster (~1 rev/day) — reflects the two dominant orbital populations.
MEO Population Note: The 1,392 MEO satellites are dominated by GNSS navigation constellations (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou) plus the Iridium and Globalstar communications networks. These operate in stable, internationally coordinated shells between approximately 2,000 km and 35,000 km altitude.
3

Major Constellation & Operator Breakdown

Constellation identification is performed by parsing OBJECT_NAME prefixes. SpaceX Starlink accounts for 10,083 satellites — 67.8% of the entire active catalog — representing a concentration of orbital infrastructure unprecedented in the history of spaceflight. The next largest single operator, OneWeb, manages 651 satellites (4.4%), less than 1/15th of Starlink's size.

The "Other/Independent" bucket (2,796 satellites, 18.8%) encompasses a broad range of government, commercial, and academic spacecraft without standardised naming prefixes — including weather satellites, Earth observation platforms, technology demonstrators, and military reconnaissance payloads.

Statistical Skew Warning: Any mean, median, or distribution computed across the full catalog is heavily biased by Starlink. The fleet median inclination of 53.16° reflects Starlink's primary 53° orbital shell. Analysts should routinely segment Starlink vs. non-Starlink to draw policy-relevant conclusions.
Top 15 Constellations / Operators by Satellite Count
Parsed from OBJECT_NAME prefixes. "Other/Independent" = named objects without a recognized constellation prefix.
# Constellation / Operator Count Share of Total Scale

Chinese constellation activity is notable across multiple programs: Yaogan reconnaissance (165), G60/Qianfan broadband internet (267 combined), Jilin-1 Earth observation (59), GeeSAT (63), and BeiDou navigation (55) together total approximately 609 satellites — the second-largest national presence after the United States.

4

Launch Year Trends

Launch year is extracted from the first four characters of the OBJECT_ID field (format: YYYY-NNNXXX). The resulting time series reveals a structural break around 2019–2020 when SpaceX began mass-deploying Starlink. Annual launch counts of currently-active satellites increased from ~150 in 2019 to 4,329 in 2025 — a 28× acceleration in six years. The 2026 figure (962) is a partial-year count through late March.

The cumulative active fleet grew from approximately 1,414 satellites at end-2019 to 14,875 by early 2026 — a 10.5× increase in under seven years. This growth rate has no historical precedent and presents the most pressing challenge for orbital spectrum management, debris risk assessment, and international coordination frameworks.

Annual Launch Count of Currently-Active Satellites (2010–2026)
Bar = satellites launched that year still active in 2026. Line = cumulative total. 2026 is a partial year (through ~Mar 30).
Cumulative Active Fleet Growth (2010–2026)
The inflection point is unmistakable: exponential growth begins in 2020 with Starlink's first operational launches.
Pre-2020 vs. Post-2020 Active Fleet
90.5% of all currently active satellites were launched in 2020 or later. The pre-2020 heritage fleet represents just 9.5% of the catalog.
Key Inflection Points: 2020 marked the first year Starlink batch launches became routine (498 active survivors). 2021–2022 saw expansion to multiple shells. 2023–2024 added competing constellations (OneWeb, Kuiper, Chinese programs). 2025's record 4,329 reflects both continued Starlink expansion and the acceleration of rival broadband networks.
5

Orbital Parameter Deep Dive

Three primary orbital parameters — inclination, eccentricity, and mean motion — characterize the geometry and altitude of each orbit. Their distributions are strongly shaped by the dominant constellation populations.

Inclination Distribution

SpaceX Starlink accounts for 10,083 satellites — 67.8% of the entire active catalog — representing a concentration of orbital infrastructure unprecedented in the history of spaceflight. The next largest single operator, OneWeb, manages 651 satellites (4.4%), less than 1/15th of Starlink's size.

The "Other/Independent" bucket (2,796 satellites, 18.8%) encompasses a broad range of government, commercial, and academic spacecraft without standardised naming prefixes — including weather satellites, Earth observation platforms, technology demonstrators, and military reconnaissance payloads.

4

Launch Year Trends

Launch year is extracted from the first four characters of the OBJECT_ID field (format: YYYY-NNNXXX). The resulting time series reveals a structural break around 2019–2020 when SpaceX began mass-deploying Starlink. Annual launch counts of currently-active satellites increased from ~150 in 2019 to 4,329 in 2025 — a 28× acceleration in six years. The 2026 figure (962) is a partial-year count through late March.

The cumulative active fleet grew from approximately 1,414 satellites at end-2019 to 14,875 by early 2026 — a 10.5× increase in under seven years. This growth rate has no historical precedent and presents the most pressing challenge for orbital spectrum management, debris risk assessment, and international coordination frameworks.

Orbital Parameter Deep Dive

Three primary orbital parameters — inclination, eccentricity, and mean motion — characterize the geometry and altitude of each orbit. Their distributions are strongly shaped by the dominant constellation populations.

Inclination Distribution
Orbital tilt relative to equator. The 45–55° spike reflects Starlink's primary 53° shell; the 80–100° peak represents sun-synchronous LEO imagery satellites.
Eccentricity Distribution
99.0% of active satellites have eccentricity < 0.01 (near-circular). Only 41 have eccentricity > 0.1 — these are HEO and legacy science orbiters.

Regime clusters are visible: LEO (high MM, ~45–90°), GEO (MM ~1, <15°), MEO (intermediate MM, ~55–65°).

Inclination clusters: The 45–55° bin (5,495 satellites) is dominated by Starlink's 53° operational shell. The 30–45° range (3,880) reflects OneWeb (87.4°), Kuiper (51.9°), and various national programs. The 80–100° bin (2,809 + 1,075 = 3,884) is characteristic of sun-synchronous polar orbits used by Earth observation satellites — orbits that precess at ~1°/day to maintain a constant Sun-angle across the ground track.

Eccentricity: The concentration of 13,694 satellites (92.1%) in the 0.000–0.001 band confirms that virtually all active satellites maintain nearly circular orbits. The 32 satellites with eccentricity > 0.5 are primarily Cold War-era payloads, Molniya communication satellites, and specialized science missions requiring high-apogee passes over particular geographic regions.

Key Takeaways & Outlook

The 2026 satellite catalog documents a space environment undergoing a rapid and historically singular transformation. The following takeaways are directly grounded in the data and carry direct implications for spectrum governance, orbital debris policy, and constellation licensing.

🛰️
Single-Operator Concentration Risk
SpaceX Starlink operates 10,083 of 14,875 active satellites (67.8%). A single operator's technical or business decisions — changes to constellation design, deorbit behavior, or frequency coordination — now have systemic consequences for the global orbital environment. Regulatory frameworks premised on a diversified operator landscape require re-examination.
📈
Irreversible LEO Densification
90.5% of active satellites were launched since 2020. The LEO shell between 530–570 km (Starlink's primary shell) has experienced a density increase unmatched in orbital history. Collision probability and conjunction frequency in this altitude band have increased commensurately, elevating the systemic risk of a Kessler-type cascade.
🌐
Spectrum Congestion at 53° Inclination
The 45–55° inclination bin contains 5,495 satellites — 37% of the active fleet — concentrated in a narrow orbital band. Ku/Ka-band downlink competition, inter-satellite link coordination, and ground-station time allocation at mid-latitudes are already constrained and will intensify as Kuiper and Chinese broadband networks grow.
🇨🇳
Emerging Chinese Mega-Constellation Pressure
G60/Qianfan, GeeSAT, Jilin-1, and other Chinese programs collectively represent ~609 active satellites, with stated constellation targets exceeding 10,000 spacecraft. The trajectory of Chinese broadband LEO deployment suggests a second major population surge comparable to Starlink's 2020–2025 growth phase is imminent.
⚖️
GEO Remains Strategically Important
Despite representing only 4.0% of active satellites (596 spacecraft), GEO remains irreplaceable for broadcast, weather, and military communications requiring coverage of fixed geographic areas without constellation overhead. The GEO arc is effectively full; any new GEO filing must displace or coordinate with existing operators.
🔭
HEO / Legacy Heritage Fleet
Only 16 satellites meet the HEO classification threshold (Molniya-type, eccentricity > 0.3, MM 1.8–3.0 rev/day). The broader heritage fleet — objects launched before 2000 still tracked as active — numbers only ~115 records, underscoring that the active catalog is predominantly a post-2020 phenomenon.
Policy Recommendation Focus Areas: (1) Binding post-mission disposal rules for LEO constellations with quantified deorbit timelines; (2) ITU spectrum filing reform to prevent paper satellite filings that "squat" orbital positions; (3) Standardized conjunction data sharing requirements for all licensed operators; (4) Bilateral and multilateral coordination mechanisms for the Starlink/Chinese broadband overlap in the 530–570 km shell.
